The '''Upper East Side''' (sometimes abbreviated '''UES''') is a neighborhood in the [[Boroughs of New York City|borough]] of [[Manhattan]] in [[New York City]]. It is bounded approximately by [[96th Street (Manhattan)|96th Street]] to the north, the [[East River]] to the east, [[59th Street (Manhattan)|59th Street]] to the south, and [[Central Park]] and [[Fifth Avenue]] to the west.<ref>Gronowicz, Anthony. ""Upper East Side in {{cite enc-nyc2}} p. 1352</ref> The neighborhood area incorporates several smaller neighborhoods, including [[Lenox Hill]], [[Carnegie Hill]], and [[Yorkville, Manhattan|Yorkville]]. Once known as the [[Stocking|Silk Stocking]] District,<ref name="two">[http://www.thecityreview.com/uesintro.html The City Review] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110628213734/http://www.thecityreview.com/uesintro.html |date=June 28, 2011 }} Upper East Side, the Silk Stocking District</ref> it has long been the wealthiest neighborhood in New York City.<ref>Plitt, Amy. [https://ny.curbed.com/2017/6/27/15881706/nyc-richest-neighborhoods-manhattan-brooklyn "The richest neighborhoods in New York City; Where do the wealthiest New Yorkers live? The answers may surprise you (or not)"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170904105530/https://ny.curbed.com/2017/6/27/15881706/nyc-richest-neighborhoods-manhattan-brooklyn |date=September 4, 2017 }}, [[Curbed]] New York, June 27, 2017. Accessed September 3, 2017. "That the Upper East Side is No. 1 should come as no surprise, given the concentration of wealth found along the westernmost border of the neighborhood (i. e., Museum Mile and the Gold Coast)."</ref>

The Upper East Side is part of [[Manhattan Community Board 8|Manhattan Community District 8]], and its primary [[ZIP Code]]s are 10021, 10028, 10065, 10075, and 10128.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the 19th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department]].

==Geography==
Neighborhood boundaries in [[New York City]] are not officially set, but according to the ''[[Encyclopedia of New York City]]'', the Upper East Side is bounded by [[59th Street (Manhattan)|59th Street]] in the south, [[96th Street (Manhattan)|96th Street]] on the north, [[Fifth Avenue]] to the west, and the [[East River]] to the east.<ref name=encnyc>Gronowicz, Anthony. "Upper East Side" in {{cite enc-nyc2|page=1352}}</ref> The ''[[AIA Guide to New York City]]'' extends the northern boundary to [[106th Street (Manhattan)|106th Street]] near Fifth Avenue.<ref name=aia5>{{cite aia5|page=416}}</ref>

The area's north–south avenues are [[Fifth Avenue|Fifth]], [[Madison Avenue|Madison]], [[Park Avenue|Park]], [[Lexington Avenue|Lexington]], [[Third Avenue|Third]], [[Second Avenue (Manhattan)|Second]], [[First Avenue (Manhattan)|First]], [[York Avenue|York]], and [[East End Avenue]]s, with the latter running only from East [[79th Street (Manhattan)|79th Street]] to [[90th Street (Manhattan)|East 90th Street]]. The major east–west streets are 59th Street, [[72nd Street (Manhattan)|72nd Street]], 79th Street, [[86th Street (Manhattan)|86th Street]], and 96th Street.

Some real-estate agents use the term "Upper East Side", instead of "[[East Harlem]]", to describe areas that are slightly north of 96th Street and near Fifth Avenue, in order to avoid associating these areas with the negative connotations of the latter, a neighborhood which is generally perceived as less prestigious.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/01/31/realestate/is-the-upper-east-side-moving-north.html?pagewanted=1 |title=Is the Upper East Side Moving North? |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=January 31, 1988 |access-date=May 12, 2011 |first=Anthony |last=DePalma |archive-date=January 21, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140121062421/http://www.nytimes.com/1988/01/31/realestate/is-the-upper-east-side-moving-north.html?pagewanted=1 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Historic districts ===
[[File:1030 Fifth Avenue (51333721980).jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|The Metropolitan Museum Historic District, designed in 1977]]
The [[Upper East Side Historic District]] was designated as a city district in 1981<ref name="NYCL-1081" /> and listed on the [[National Register of Historic Places]] in 1984.<ref>[http://www.nyc.gov/html/lpc/downloads/pdf/reports/UpperEastSide_Vol1.pdf Upper East Side Historic District Designation Report, Vol. 1] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170225174746/http://www.nyc.gov/html/lpc/downloads/pdf/reports/UpperEastSide_Vol1.pdf |date=February 25, 2017 }}, May 19, 1981, [[Landmarks Preservation Commission]]</ref> The city district runs from 59th to 78th Streets along Fifth Avenue, and up to Third Avenue at some points.<ref name="NYCL-1081">{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/1051.pdf|title=Upper East Side Historic District|date=May 19, 1981|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=2019-12-06|archive-date=September 21, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921134220/https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/1051.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|3}} It is composed of residential structures built after the [[American Civil War]]; mansions and townhouses built at the beginning of the 20th century; and apartment buildings erected later on.<ref name="NYCL-1081"/><ref>{{Cite journal|url =http://www.citi-habitats.com/media/guides/upper_east_side.pdf|title =The Upper East Side|date =2007|journal =Citi Habitats|url-status =dead|archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20120917041214/http://www.citi-habitats.com/media/guides/upper_east_side.pdf|archive-date =September 17, 2012|df =mdy-all}}</ref> The city district was slightly expanded in 2010 with 74 additional buildings.<ref name="NYCL-2373">{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2373.pdf|title=Upper East Side Historic District Extension|date=March 23, 2010|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=2019-12-06|archive-date=September 21, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921133759/https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2373.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|4}}

The Metropolitan Museum Historic District was designated a city district in 1977. It consists of properties on Fifth Avenue between 79th and 86th Streets, outside the [[Metropolitan Museum of Art]], as well as properties on several side streets.<ref name="NYCL-0955">{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0955.pdf|title=Metropolitan Museum Historic District|date=September 20, 1977|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=2019-12-06|archive-date=September 21, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921131109/https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0955.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|2}}

The Park Avenue Historic District was designated a city district in 2014. It encompasses 64 properties on Park Avenue between 79th and 91st Streets.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2547.pdf|title=Park Avenue Historic District|date=April 29, 2014|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=2019-12-14|archive-date=August 24, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210824220010/http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/2547.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|4}}

The [[Carnegie Hill Historic District]] was designated a city district in 1974 and expanded in 1993. It covers 400 buildings, primarily along Fifth Avenue from 86th to 98th Street, as well as on side streets extending east to Madison, Park, and Lexington Avenues.<ref name="NYCL-1834">{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/1834.pdf|title=Expanded Carnegie Hill Historic District|date=December 21, 1993|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=2019-12-06|archive-date=September 21, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921130753/https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/1834.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>{{Rp|3}}

There are also two smaller city historic districts. The [[Henderson Place Historic District]], designated in 1969, comprises the town houses on East End Avenue between 86th and 87th Streets, built by John C. Henderson in 1981.<ref name="NYCL-04543">{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0454.pdf|title=Henderson Place Historic District|date=February 11, 1969|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=2019-12-06|archive-date=October 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211017125644/https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0454.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> The [[Treadwell Farm Historic District]], designated in 1967, includes low-rise apartments on East 61st and 62nd Streets between Second and Third Avenues, on the former farm of Adam Treadwell.<ref name="NYCL-0536">{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0536.pdf|title=Treadwell Farm Historic District|date=December 13, 1967|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=2019-12-06|archive-date=October 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211017122122/https://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0536.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

==History==
===Development===
[[File:Gracie East front summer jeh.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|[[Gracie Mansion]], the official residence of the [[Mayor of New York City]] and the city's last remaining [[East River]] villa]]
Before the arrival of Europeans, the mouths of streams<ref>Noted at East 53rd, 62nd, [[74th Street (Manhattan)|74th Streets]] (the Saw Kill, dammed to form the [[The Ramble and Lake|Lake in Central Park]]) and 80th Street (Eric W. Sanderson, ''Mannahatta: A Natural History of New York City'', 2009, p. 261 "Lenape sites and place-names").</ref> that eroded gullies in the East River bluffs are conjectured to have been the sites of fishing camps used by the [[Lenape]], whose [[controlled burns]] once a generation or so kept the dense canopy of [[oak–hickory forest]] open at ground level.<ref>A reconstructed map of the patchwork ecologies of Manhattan island before Europeanization is presented in Sanderson 2009; map p. 139.</ref>

In the 19th century{{Efn|The history of the Upper East Side, in the broader citywide context, is repeatedly noted in {{Cite gotham}}}} the farmland and market garden district of what was to be the Upper East Side was still traversed by the [[Boston Post Road]] and, from 1837, the [[New York and Harlem Railroad]], which brought straggling commercial development around its one station in the neighborhood, at 86th Street, which became the heart of German [[Yorkville, Manhattan|Yorkville]]. The area was defined by the attractions of the bluff overlooking the [[East River]], which ran without interruption from [[James William Beekman]]'s "Mount Pleasant", north of the marshy squalor of [[Turtle Bay, Manhattan|Turtle Bay]], to [[Gracie Mansion]], north of which the land sloped steeply to the wetlands that separated this area from the suburban village of [[Harlem]].<ref>The original ecology of Manhattan Island and its evolution is now thoroughly explored in [[Eric W. ===Arrival of famous residents===
Before the [[Park Avenue Tunnel (railroad)|Park Avenue Tunnel]] was covered (finished in 1910), fashionable New Yorkers shunned the smoky railroad trench up Fourth Avenue (now Park Avenue), to build stylish mansions and [[townhouse]]s on the large lots along [[Fifth Avenue]], facing Central Park, and on the adjacent side streets. The latest arrivals were the rich Pittsburghers [[Andrew Carnegie]] and [[Henry Clay Frick]]. The classic phase of [[Gilded Age]] Fifth Avenue as a stretch of private mansions was not long-lasting: the first apartment house to replace a private mansion on upper Fifth Avenue was [[907 Fifth Avenue]] (1916), at 72nd Street, the neighborhood's grand carriage entrance to Central Park.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thecityreview.com/ues/fifave/fif907.htm |title=The Upper East Side Book: 907 Fifth Avenue |publisher=Thecityreview.com |date=July 31, 2010 |access-date=May 12, 2011 |archive-date=September 22, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200922014020/https://www.thecityreview.com/ues/fifave/fif907.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

Most members of New York's upper-class families have made residences on the Upper East Side, including the oil-rich [[Rockefeller family|Rockefellers]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thecityreview.com/ues/fifave/fif834.htm |title=The Upper East Side Book: Fifth Avenue: 834 Fifth Avenue |publisher=Thecityreview.com |access-date=May 12, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110526194733/http://www.thecityreview.com/ues/fifave/fif834.htm |archive-date=May 26, 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref> political [[Roosevelt family|Roosevelts]], [[political family|political dynastic]] [[Kennedy family|Kennedys]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.closmimi.com/carlylehotel.php |title=Clos Mimi |publisher=Clos Mimi |date=March 22, 2007 |access-date=May 12, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110426184633/http://www.closmimi.com/carlylehotel.php |archive-date=April 26, 2011 }}</ref> [[thoroughbred]] racing moneyed [[Whitney family|Whitneys]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thecityreview.com/ues/fifave/fif1125.htm |title=The Upper East Side Book: Fifth Avenue: 1125 Fifth Avenue |publisher=Thecityreview.com |access-date=May 12, 2011 |archive-date=May 26, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110526195833/http://www.thecityreview.com/ues/fifave/fif1125.htm |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1907/05/26/106708633.pdf |title=Natives of New York Still Own Upper Fifth Avenue – In Spite of the Influx of Outsiders, Knickerbocker Families Easily Remain In the Ascendant. The Majority, Who Are Not Knickerbockers, Hail from New England and the Eastern States | work = [[The New York Times]] |date=May 26, 1907 |access-date=May 12, 2011}}</ref> and [[tobacco]] and [[electric power]] fortuned [[James Buchanan Duke|Dukes]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.divasthesite.com/Society_Divas/doris_duke_a.htm |title=at |publisher=Divasthesite.com |access-date=May 12, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100728092720/http://www.divasthesite.com/Society_Divas/doris_duke_a.htm |archive-date=July 28, 2010 }}</ref>

===Transportation constructed===
[[File:45 East 66th Street.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|alt=45 East 66th Street, a designated New York City landmark|[[45 East 66th Street]], a designated [[New York City landmark]], as seen from [[Madison Avenue]]]]
[[File:MMPU hall 209 E85 jeh.JPG|thumb|upright=1.1|The [[Musical Mutual Protective Union]] on [[85th Street (Manhattan)|85th Street]]]]
Construction of the [[IRT Third Avenue Line|Third Avenue El]], opened from 1878 in sections, followed by the [[IRT Second Avenue Line|Second Avenue El]], opened in 1879, linked the Upper East Side's middle class and skilled artisans closely to the heart of the city, and confirmed the modest nature of the area to their east. The unbuilt "Hamilton Square",<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-08-18 |title=The Past Life of CUNY's Hunter College: The Lost Hamilton Square in NYC |url=https://untappedcities.com/2015/08/18/the-past-life-of-cunys-hunter-college-the-lost-hamilton-square-in-nyc/ |access-date=2022-06-22 |website=Untapped New York |language=en-US |archive-date=August 13, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220813101753/https://untappedcities.com/2015/08/18/the-past-life-of-cunys-hunter-college-the-lost-hamilton-square-in-nyc/ |url-status=live }}</ref> which had appeared as one of the few genteel interruptions of the grid plan on [[city map]]s since the [[Commissioners' Plan of 1811]], was intended to straddle what had now become the Harlem Railroad right-of-way between 66th and 69th Streets; it never materialized, though during the [[Panic of 1857]] its unleveled ground was the scene of an open-air mass meeting called in July to agitate for the secession of the city and its neighboring counties from New York State, and the city divided its acreage into house lots and sold them.<ref>Edwin G. Burrows and Mike Wallace, ''Gotham: a history of New York City to 1898'', 1999, pp. 421, 840, 849.</ref> From the 1880s the neighborhood of [[Yorkville, Manhattan|Yorkville]] became a suburb of middle class Germans.<ref>{{Cite book | author = Croton-On-Hudson Historical Society |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=B1OcxFn5xB0C|title=Images of America Series | publisher = Arcadia Publishing | year = 2001 | pages = 41, 128 | isbn = 0738505439}}</ref>

[[Gracie Mansion]], the last remaining suburban villa overlooking the East River at [[Carl Schurz Park]], became the home of New York's [[Mayors of New York City|mayor]] in 1942.<ref>Barron, james; and Roberts, Sam. The racial composition of the Upper East Side changed moderately from 2000 to 2010. === Ethnic and socioeconomic trends ===
As of the 2000 census, twenty-one percent of the population was foreign born; of this, 45.6% came from Europe, 29.5% from Asia, 16.2% from Latin America and 8.7% from other areas. The female-male ratio was very high with 125 females for 100 males.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.socialexplorer.com/pub/maps/map3.aspx?g=0&mapi=SE0012&themei=767694.920954384.6460.988&l=2283243.52287408&r=2291023.93491898&t=5256165.51580534&b=5251538.1864453&rndi=1 |title=Social Explorer 2000 Demography Map: Median Income in Upper East Side |publisher=Socialexplorer.com |access-date=May 12, 2011 }}{{Dead link|date=May 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> The Upper East Side contains a large and affluent [[American Jews|Jewish]] population estimated at 56,000.<ref name="lub1">{{cite web|url=http://lubavitch.com/news/article/2030659/Jewish-Identity-Grows-On-Manhattans-Upper-East-Side.html|title=Jewish Identity Grows On Manhattan's Upper East Side|author=Baila Olidort|publisher=lubavitch.com|date=February 17, 2014|access-date=June 23, 2014|archive-date=May 4, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140504202108/http://lubavitch.com/news/article/2030659/Jewish-Identity-Grows-On-Manhattans-Upper-East-Side.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Traditionally, the Upper East Side has been dominated by wealthy [[White Anglo-Saxon Protestant]] families.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Craig J. Calhoun |author2= Donald Light |author3=[[Suzanne Keller]]|title=Sociology|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=dvQM-npb2akC|year=1997|page=178|publisher=McGraw-Hill|isbn= 9780070380691 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author1=Paul Schlueter|author2=Dorothy Nyren Curley|title=Modern American literature: volume V second supplement to the fourth edition|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PFofAQAAIAAJ&q=Modern+American+literature|year=1998|page=13|publisher=Gale Group|isbn=9780804432658|access-date=November 22, 2020|archive-date=April 1, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230401195003/https://books.google.com/books?id=PFofAQAAIAAJ&q=Modern+American+literature|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author1=Briton Hadden |author2= Henry Robinson Luce|title=Time, Volume 110, Edizioni 1–9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zyw7AQAAIAAJ&q=Time,+Volume+110|year=1998|page=156|publisher= Time Incorporated}}</ref>

Given its very high population density and per capita income ($85,081 in 2000), the neighborhood contains the greatest concentration of individual wealth in Manhattan. As of 2011, the median household income for the Upper East Side was $131,492.<ref name="stats" /> The Upper East Side maintains the highest pricing per square foot in the United States. A 2002 report cited the average cost per square meter as $8,856; however, that price has seen a substantial jump, increasing to almost as much as $11,200 per square meter as of 2006. There are some buildings which cost about $125 per square foot (~$1345/ m<sup>2</sup>).<ref>{{cite news |last=Hevesi |first=Dennis |date=May 17, 2002 |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9D06E6DF1F39F934A25756C0A9649C8B63 |title=Residential Real Estate; TriBeCa Is Priciest Neighborhood |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071017220131/http://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9D06E6DF1F39F934A25756C0A9649C8B63 |archive-date=October 17, 2007 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=June 7, 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.millersamuel.com/charts/gallery-view.php?ViewNode=1155055479AKfgw&Record=33 |title=Charts |publisher=Miller Samuel |date=February 14, 2011 |access-date=May 12, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714094629/http://www.millersamuel.com/charts/gallery-view.php?ViewNode=1155055479AKfgw&Record=33 |archive-date=July 14, 2011 }}</ref> The only [[public housing]] projects for those of low to moderate incomes on the Upper East Side are located just south of the neighborhood's northern limit at 96th Street, the [[Holmes Towers]] and [[Isaacs Houses]]. It borders [[East Harlem]], which has the highest concentration of public housing in the United States.<ref>{{cite web|last=Mays|first=Jeff|date=April 14, 2011|title=Low-Income Parents Worry Cuts to Childcare Will Force Them Out of Work|url=http://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20110414/harlem/lowincome-parents-worry-cuts-childcare-will-force-them-out-of-work|website=DNAinfo New York|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121008003622/http://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20110414/harlem/lowincome-parents-worry-cuts-childcare-will-force-them-out-of-work|archive-date=October 8, 2012}}</ref>

==Police and crime==
The Upper East Side is patrolled by the 19th Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 153 East 67th Street.<ref name="NYPD 19th Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/19th-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 19th Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016|archive-date=June 5, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170605034846/http://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/19th-precinct.page|url-status=live}}</ref> The 19th Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 82.2% between 1990 and 2022. The precinct reported 2 murders, 12 rapes, 229 robberies, 173 felony assaults, 278 burglaries, 1,724 grand larcenies, and 192 grand larcenies auto in 2022.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-019pct.pdf|title=19th Precinct CompStat Report|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=March 14, 2020|archive-date=January 3, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200103064412/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-019pct.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

{{as of|2018}}, Manhattan Community District 8 has a non-fatal assault hospitalization rate of 15 per 100,000 people, compared to the boroughwide rate of 49 per 100,000 and the citywide rate of 59 per 100,000. Its incarceration rate is 71 per 100,000 people, the lowest in the city, compared to the boroughwide rate of 407 per 100,000 and the citywide rate of 425 per 100,000.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|8}} Of the five major violent felonies (murder, rape, felony assault, robbery, and burglary), the 19th Precinct had a rate of 264 crimes per 100,000 residents in 2019, compared to the boroughwide average of 632 crimes per 100,000 and the citywide average of 572 crimes per 100,000.<ref name = "crime map"/><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/analysis_and_planning/historical-crime-data/seven-major-felony-offenses-2000-2019.pdf | title = Citywide Seven Major Felony Offenses 2000–2019 | publisher = [[New York Police Department]] | access-date = March 23, 2020 | website = www.nyc.gov | archive-date = February 17, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200217164041/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/analysis_and_planning/historical-crime-data/seven-major-felony-offenses-2000-2019.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/analysis_and_planning/historical-crime-data/seven-major-felony-offenses-by-precinct-2000-2019.pdf | title = Citywide Seven Major Felony Offenses by Precinct 2000–2019 | publisher = [[New York Police Department]] | access-date = March 23, 2020 | website = www.nyc.gov | archive-date = March 19, 2020 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200319015709/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/analysis_and_planning/historical-crime-data/seven-major-felony-offenses-by-precinct-2000-2019.pdf | url-status = live }}</ref>

==Health==
[[File:Cornell med 02.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|[[Weill Cornell Medical Center]] on East 68th Street]]
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s and births to teenage mothers on the Upper East Side are lower than the city average. On the Upper East Side, there were 73 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 3.4 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} The Upper East Side has a low population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]]. In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 4%, less than the citywide rate of 12%, though this was based on a small sample size.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], on the Upper East Side is {{convert|0.0083|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, more than the city average.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Eight percent of Upper East Side residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is less than the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} On the Upper East Side, 11% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 4% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 15% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 24%, 11%, and 28% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 6% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Ninety-four percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is higher than the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 89% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", more than the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket on the Upper East Side, there are 5 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

[[Lenox Hill Hospital]], [[NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital]], and [[Weill Cornell Medical Center]] are located on the Upper East Side. In addition, [[Mount Sinai Hospital (Manhattan)|Mount Sinai Hospital]] and [[Metropolitan Hospital Center]] are located nearby in [[East Harlem]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Manhattan Hospital Listings | website=New York Hospitals | url=http://www.allny.com/health/hosp-manhattan.html | access-date=March 20, 2019 | archive-date=November 15, 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161115151717/http://www.allny.com/health/hosp-manhattan.html | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Best Hospitals in New York, N.Y. | website=U.S. News & World Report | date=July 26, 2011 | url=https://health.usnews.com/best-hospitals/area/new-york-ny | access-date=March 20, 2019 | archive-date=May 29, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190529091928/https://health.usnews.com/best-hospitals/area/new-york-ny | url-status=live }}</ref>

== Education ==
The Upper East Side generally has a higher rate of college-educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. A majority of residents age 25 and older (83%) have a college education or higher, while 3% have less than a high school education and 14% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 64% of Manhattan residents and 43% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} The percentage of the Upper East Side students excelling in math rose from 61% in 2000 to 80% in 2011, and reading achievement increased from 66% to 68% during the same time period.<ref name=":17">{{Cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/MN_08_11.pdf|title=Upper East Side – MN 08|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016|archive-date=September 18, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130918132004/http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/MN_08_11.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

The Upper East Side's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is lower than the rest of New York City. On the Upper East Side, 8% of elementary school students missed twenty or more days per [[school year]], less than the citywide average of 20%.<ref name=":21" />{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 91% of high school students on the Upper East Side graduate on time, more than the citywide average of 75%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}

The [[New York Public Library]] (NYPL) operates four branches on the Upper East Side.
* The 67th Street branch is located at 328 East 67th Street. The branch, a [[Carnegie library]], opened in 1905 and was restored in the 1950s and in 2000. The two-story, {{convert|14000|ft2|m2|adj=on}} structure resembles the Yorkville branch library in design.<ref>{{cite web | title=About the 67th Street Library | website=The New York Public Library | date=May 10, 1907 | url=https://www.nypl.org/about/locations/67th-street | access-date=March 23, 2019 | archive-date=March 25, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190325003713/https://www.nypl.org/about/locations/67th-street | url-status=live }}</ref>
* The [[New York Public Library Yorkville Branch|Yorkville branch]] is located at 222 East 79th Street. The branch, a Carnegie library, opened in 1902 and was renovated in 1986–1987. The three-story space is listed on the [[New York State Register of Historic Places]] and the [[National Register of Historic Places]].<ref>{{cite web | title=About the Yorkville Library | website=The New York Public Library | date=May 10, 1907 | url=https://www.nypl.org/about/locations/yorkville | access-date=March 23, 2019 | archive-date=March 25, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190325003712/https://www.nypl.org/about/locations/yorkville | url-status=live }}</ref>
* The Webster branch is located at 1465 York Avenue. The branch was founded in 1893 as the Webster Free Library, and the current Carnegie library structure opened in 1906.<ref>{{cite web | title=About the Webster Library | website=The New York Public Library | date=May 10, 1907 | url=https://www.nypl.org/about/locations/webster | access-date=March 23, 2019 | archive-date=May 4, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190504211947/https://www.nypl.org/about/locations/webster | url-status=live }}</ref>
* The 96th Street branch is located at 112 East 96th Street. ==Transportation==

The Upper East Side is served by two [[New York City Subway|subway]] lines, the four-track [[IRT Lexington Avenue Line]] ({{NYCS trains|Lexington}}) under [[Lexington Avenue]] and the two-track [[Second Avenue Subway]] ({{NYCS trains|Second}}) under [[Second Avenue (Manhattan)|Second Avenue]].<ref>{{NYCS const|map}}</ref>

The Second Avenue Line serves to relieve congestion on the Lexington Avenue Line. The first phase of the line opened on January 1, 2017, consisting of three stations on the Upper East Side: [[96th Street (Second Avenue Subway)|96th Street]], [[86th Street (Second Avenue Subway)|86th Street]], and [[72nd Street (Second Avenue Subway)|72nd Street]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nbcnewyork.com/news/local/NYC-Second-Avenue-Subway-Service-Begins-January-Gov-Cuomo-Says-407383455.html|title=2nd Avenue Subway Service to Begin New Year's Day: Gov.
